title: Trump’s Back Door Into the Newsroom
author: Brian Hudson
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-22-at-12.00.03-PM-680x386.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/23/trumps-
back-door-into-the-newsroom/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-22-at-12.00.03-PM-680x386.png)

File photo of Max Blumenthal. Photo Credit: Ben Norton, Wikipedia Commons

The seizure of Max Blumenthal’s phones shows how the war on Iran and the
border-security state can turn foreign conflict into domestic repression.

Max Blumenthal returned from a reporting trip to Iran and left Washington
Dulles International Airport without the two phones that contained much of his
working life. According to a [federal filing submitted on his
behalf](https://adc.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/002-Memorandum-in-
Support.pdf), U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers questioned him about
his journalism, funding, and travel plans and seized the devices after he
declined to provide their passcodes. The [Committee to Protect Journalists
called the episode alarming](https://cpj.org/2026/07/max-blumenthal-grayzone-
founder-and-editor-in-chief-interrogated-over-reporting-assignment-to-iran/).
What happened at Dulles exposed how war abroad, exceptional border powers, and
hostility toward dissenting media can converge in a single act of state
pressure.

A journalist’s phone is no longer merely a personal device. It may be a
notebook, archive, contact list, secure mailbox, and map of confidential
relationships. Seizing it for possible data extraction is closer to searching
a newsroom than inspecting ordinary luggage. The government can enter not
through the front door with a warrant, but through the legal back door of the
border exception.

The filing says Blumenthal’s phones contained information identifying
confidential sources, unpublished reporting, and years of protected
newsgathering. Those claims have not yet been tested in court, and there is no
public evidence that Donald Trump personally ordered the seizure. A serious
defense of press freedom should not depend on exaggeration. The danger is
narrower but profound: a federal agency used broad border authority against a
journalist returning from a country with which the United States was at war
and took devices that allegedly contained source-identifying information,
confidential communications, and unpublished work.

Defending Blumenthal’s rights does not require endorsing every article or
editorial judgment associated with The Grayzone. Critics are free to challenge
his record. Constitutional protections matter most when they extend to
journalists who are controversial or distrusted by powerful institutions. If
the state may decide who qualifies as a “real” journalist before honoring
press freedom, then press freedom becomes a license for the politically
acceptable.

Supporters of broad border authority will argue that the government needs
latitude to search electronic devices to combat terrorism, smuggling, and
other transnational crimes. [CBP says officers may examine phones, computers,
cameras, and other devices at ports of entry](https://www.cbp.gov/travel/cbp-
search-authority/border-search-electronic-devices). That power can serve
legitimate purposes. But the existence of lawful authority does not make every
use of it justified—or constitutional. CBP’s own policy classifies the use of
external extraction equipment as an “advanced” search, requiring reasonable
suspicion of a legal violation or a national-security concern and senior-level
approval. Whether those standards were met in Blumenthal’s case has not been
publicly explained. When the traveler is a reporter returning from a country
Washington defines as an enemy, the device may contain source identities, raw
interviews, unpublished images, and future investigations. At that point, a
border search can become an intervention in the production of news.

The deeper problem is the widening gap between old legal categories and
digital journalism. Searching a reporter’s home or office inside the country
would normally trigger demands for judicial oversight. Yet the same
professional archive can fit inside a phone carried through an airport, where
Fourth Amendment protections remain sharply contested and executive power is
broader. The Electronic Frontier Foundation [argues that electronic-device
searches at the border should require a
warrant](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/03/eff-third-circuit-electronic-
device-searches-border-require-warrant) because modern phones contain an
extraordinary volume of personal and professional information. Without such
safeguards, the border creates legal arbitrage for the security state:
information difficult to obtain through the front door may be reached more
easily by waiting at the airport.

Trump did not invent the border exception or the national-security state’s
hostility toward leaks and dissent. Republican and Democratic administrations
built the machinery he now commands. The Obama administration, for example,
[secretly subpoenaed and seized journalists’ phone and email records during
leak investigations](https://cpj.org/reports/2013/10/obama-and-the-press-us-
leaks-surveillance-post-911/), helping normalize the treatment of
newsgathering as a target of national-security enforcement. Trump’s
distinctive contribution has been to fuse those inherited powers with an
openly retaliatory politics—one that treats criticism of a live war not merely
as opposition, but as disloyalty.

That danger cannot be separated from Trump’s conduct during the Iran war. His
Justice Department [subpoenaed The Wall Street Journal for reporters’
records](https://cpj.org/2026/05/cpj-condemns-trumps-order-for-doj-to-
subpoena-journalists/) tied to a story about Pentagon warnings over the risks
of a prolonged military campaign. The department also [issued subpoenas
seeking testimony from Washington Post and Wall Street Journal
reporters](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/06/23/doj-
issued-then-withdrew-subpoenas-force-post-wsj-reporters-testify/), then
withdrew them after legal challenges by the news organizations. Trump later
[called New York Times reporter David Sanger
“treasonous”](https://www.c-span.org/clip/white-house-event/trump-calls-ny-
times-reporter-treasonous-for-questioning-iran-war-success/5200348) after
Sanger challenged the administration’s portrayal of the war. These episodes do
not prove that Trump directed the seizure of Blumenthal’s phones. They do show
a president repeatedly recasting scrutiny of his war as disloyalty and drawing
government power into disputes that should be answered with evidence.

This is the difference between criticizing the press and weaponizing the state
against it. A president may call a story inaccurate, biased, or dishonest. But
a government must not use its powers to retaliate against journalism—or in
ways that predictably function as punishment and deterrence. Reporters can
make mistakes. The state commands prosecutors, border agents, and police
powers. Treating these as equal participants in a media argument erases the
imbalance on which authoritarian power depends.

Trump’s responsibility therefore does not begin only when someone finds his
signature on an operational order. When a president repeatedly portrays
critical reporters as traitorous enemies, he creates a permissive climate in
which agencies can treat reporting as a security threat. That is not a claim
that every official action is centrally coordinated. It is an argument about
governing incentives: language from the top tells institutions which targets
deserve suspicion and which excesses may be rewarded rather than restrained.

The Blumenthal case reveals how a subtler form of censorship can operate. An
administration need not ban travel to Iran or prohibit reporting that
challenges Washington’s narrative. It can instead raise the cost of coming
home: questioning, seized equipment, uncertain data security, legal expenses,
and frightened sources. Call it a return tax on adversarial journalism. The
formal message remains that reporters are free to travel and publish. The
practical message is that they should be prepared to surrender their mobile
newsroom at the border.

The chilling effect reaches far beyond Blumenthal. The most important audience
may be the reporter deciding whether to travel to Tehran, Gaza, Moscow,
Caracas, or another place where U.S. narratives are contested. Editors must
calculate legal and security risks. Sources must wonder whether confidential
messages will reach American authorities. Even if no data were extracted from
Blumenthal’s devices, the possibility alone can destroy trust. A phone seizure
pressures not only one individual, but an entire network of future reporting.

Courts and Congress should draw a clear line between searching ordinary
personal property and accessing a device containing confidential sources and
unpublished journalistic material. Such searches should require a specific
factual basis, judicial authorization, and an independent process to protect
newsgathering records. The border exception cannot become a permanent
workaround for the First Amendment.

The test of press freedom is not how a government treats journalists whom the
president considers fair or respectable. It is whether a reporter whose
politics, travels, and work Trump despises can reenter his own country without
surrendering his archive. War abroad comes home long before a newspaper is
closed or an editor is jailed. It begins when powers built for foreign enemies
are turned against the domestic production of knowledge. At Dulles, the border
did not merely mark the entrance to the country. It became a warning that the
security state’s back door into the newsroom is already open.
